title: RC: Believing on the word of others
passage:
There is an old and honourable ideal, associated with Locke and the early modern defenders of intellectual autonomy, according to which a rational person believes only what she has examined for herself. To take a proposition on trust, on this view, is to abdicate: the floating of other people's opinions in our brains, Locke wrote, makes us not one jot the more knowing, though they happen to be true. The ideal survives in the modern injunction to "think for yourself", and in the faint embarrassment we feel when asked why we believe something and can only answer that we read it somewhere.

The ideal is also impossible, and it is worth being precise about why. It is not merely that life is short and the sciences are long, so that no one could personally verify the boiling point of sulphur, the date of a medieval battle and the safety of the local water supply. It is that the very instruments of personal verification are themselves received on trust. The language in which I frame my doubts was taught to me; the standards by which I judge evidence were absorbed from teachers whose competence I was in no position to assess; the map I use to find the laboratory was drawn by strangers. A person who refused all testimony would not be a rigorous knower but a newborn.

Once this is granted, the interesting question changes. It is no longer whether to rely on the word of others but how, and the answer cannot be "indiscriminately". Here the autonomist has a point that should be conceded in full: deference goes wrong, and it goes wrong in characteristic ways. Communities that trust a single source lose the capacity to notice when that source fails. Expertise is borrowed by people who have none, and the borrowing is invisible to the borrower. The history of medicine before the randomised trial is largely a history of confident, well-credentialed testimony that killed its patients.

But notice what the failures have in common. They are failures in the structure of trust, not in trust as such. A community that relies on many independent sources, that rewards those who check and punishes those who are caught embellishing, that keeps open the channels through which a dissenting witness can be heard, is a community in which believing on the word of others is not a lapse of rationality but the ordinary exercise of it. What the individual cannot do, verify everything, the structure does on her behalf, provided it is well built. The rational believer is not the one who trusts least but the one who can tell a well-built structure from a badly built one.

This relocates the ethics of belief from the solitary mind to the institutions that feed it: the newsroom, the journal, the examining board, the court. It also explains why the modern anxiety about "misinformation" is misdescribed as a crisis of credulity. People have always believed what they were told; the question is what they are told, by whom, and whether the structures that once filtered testimony still function. To tell the citizen to think for herself is to hand her a task that no one has ever performed, and to let the institutions that could perform it on her behalf off the hook.

title: RC: The manufacture of the hour
passage:
Historians of industrialisation used to tell a simple story about time. Before the factory, work followed the task and the season: the harvest was brought in when it was ripe, the net mended when it tore, and the day was divided by the sun and by hunger. The factory introduced the clock, and with it a new discipline, in which labour was measured, bought and sold by the hour. On this telling, the clock was a neutral instrument that merely made visible a quantity, time, that had always been there to be measured; what changed was that employers now had a reason to measure it.

The story is not false, but it has the causation backwards. Time measured by the hour was not discovered by the factory and then exploited; it was made by it. Pre-industrial communities had clocks, some of them very good, and they used them for prayer, for markets and for the astronomy of the almanac. What they did not have, because they had no use for it, was the idea that an hour of one person's labour was interchangeable with an hour of another's, so that the two could be added, priced and compared. That idea required a mode of production in which the worker's contribution had been detached from the task and reduced to attendance. The clock did not create the abstraction; the wage relation did, and then found in the clock the instrument it needed.

It would be easy to turn this into a romance of task-oriented time, and some writers have. The pre-industrial day was not leisurely; it was long, irregular and frequently hungry, and its "natural" rhythm included the natural rhythm of debt and dearth. Nor was the factory's time-discipline simply imposed. Workers fought for the clock as often as against it: the demand for a ten-hour day, and later an eight-hour one, was a demand that time be measured accurately, because only a measured hour could be a limited one. The clock that disciplined was also the clock that protected.

Yet this concession strengthens rather than weakens the main point. If both employer and worker came to want the measured hour, for opposite reasons, then the measured hour was not a fact of nature that one side imposed on the other; it was a shared social achievement, contested in its uses but agreed in its form. The eight-hour day, which we now treat as a kind of physiological baseline, was argued for in the 1880s not from the body but from citizenship: a worker, the argument went, needed eight hours for work, eight for sleep, and eight "for what we will", the last being the hours of a free person. The number was a political claim dressed as a schedule.

What follows is a certain humility about the word "natural" as applied to work. The rhythms we feel in our bodies, the restlessness at the end of a long shift, the particular shape of a weekend, are historical products that have been lived long enough to be mistaken for biology. This does not make them arbitrary, or easily changed; a century of habit is not undone by noticing it. But it does mean that proposals to reorganise the working day, whether to four days or to none, cannot be dismissed on the ground that they violate a natural order. The order was manufactured, and what has been manufactured once can be manufactured again.

title: RC: Who corrects science?
passage:
The reassurance that science is "self-correcting" is offered so often, and so automatically, that it is worth asking what the phrase could mean. Taken literally it is false: no finding corrects itself. Taken as a claim about scientists, it is only intermittently true: the researcher who has built a career on a result is the last person motivated to overturn it, and the history of the subject is full of elderly eminences defending, to the grave, theories their students had abandoned. If science corrects itself, the self in question is not the finding and not the individual. It is the institution, and institutions correct only when they are built to.

The point matters because of the way the recent crisis of replication has been discussed. When a large fraction of published results in a field fail to reproduce, the response divides along a familiar line. Defenders say the failures are the system working: errors were published, errors were found, and the finding of them is self-correction in action. Critics say the failures show the system broken: the errors were published in the first place, and they were found only when outsiders went looking. Both sides speak as though "the system" were a single thing whose health could be read from a single number.

The defenders have the better of one argument. A field in which nothing is ever found to be wrong is not a healthy field; it is a field that has stopped checking. Replication failure is evidence of checking, and a rising rate of detected error can be a sign of improvement rather than decay, in the way that rising reported crime can reflect better policing. The critics' demand for a science without retractions is a demand for a science without tests.

But the defenders mistake a possibility for a mechanism. That errors can be caught says nothing about whether, in this field, under these incentives, they will be. The mechanism requires that someone be paid, promoted or at least not punished for the unglamorous work of repeating what has already been done; that journals publish negative results, which they mostly do not; that the data behind a claim be available to those who would check it, which until recently they mostly were not. Where these conditions fail, self-correction is not a property of science but a slogan about it. The replication crisis was not uncovered by the ordinary operation of the field; it was uncovered by a small number of researchers who chose, at some cost to themselves, to do what the incentives discouraged.

This suggests that the right response is neither reassurance nor lament but engineering. If the correction of error is an institutional product, then it can be produced more or less efficiently, and the levers are known: pre-registration of hypotheses, so that a study cannot quietly change its question after seeing its answer; mandatory sharing of data and code; journals that commit to publishing a replication whatever its result; and credit, in the currency that academic careers actually run on, for finding that a famous result is false. None of this is romantic. But the romance of the lone investigator who sees the truth that the field has missed is precisely the story that has let the field off the hook, by locating correction in a heroic individual rather than in the ordinary arrangements that make heroism unnecessary.

title: RC: The fidelity question
passage:
Reviews of translations tend to reach, sooner or later, for the vocabulary of fidelity. A translation is "faithful" or it "takes liberties"; it "betrays" the original or "serves" it; the translator is a devoted spouse or a treacherous one. The metaphor is so entrenched that it is hard to see it as a metaphor, and harder still to see what it assumes: that there exists, prior to any translation, a fixed meaning in the source text against which the translation can be measured, as a copy is measured against an original.

No one who has translated a sentence believes this for long. The source text does not hand over its meaning; it has to be read, and reading is already a choice among possibilities that the text leaves open. When the Italian says "lo spirito", the translator must decide whether the spirit in question is a ghost, a mood, a liquor or a soul, and the Italian does not say. To call one of those choices "faithful" is to say only that the critic would have chosen it too. The translation that is accused of liberties has usually taken the same number of decisions as the one praised for fidelity; it has simply taken different ones, or taken them visibly.

This is not an argument that anything goes. There are mistranslations, in the plain sense: the translator who renders a negative as a positive, or who did not know that the idiom was an idiom, has made an error, and the error can be shown. The fidelity metaphor earns its keep in such cases, and a theory of translation that could not distinguish a blunder from an interpretation would be useless. But the cases that reviews actually argue about are rarely of this kind. They concern tone, register, the decision to preserve a strangeness or to domesticate it, the choice between a rhythm and a meaning when the two cannot both survive. In these cases there is no fact of the matter that "fidelity" could track, and the word functions as a compliment or an insult wearing the costume of a measurement.

What would a better vocabulary look like? I suggest that we think of a translation as a reading, and judge it as we judge readings: not as accurate or inaccurate but as strong or weak, generous or mean, alive or inert. A strong reading of a poem is one that makes the poem more available, that finds in it something a weaker reading had left dormant, that can be argued with because it has committed itself. A strong translation does the same, in another language. It is answerable to the original, as a reading is answerable to its text; it cannot say anything it likes. But its answerability is not that of a copy, and its success is not measured by how little it has added. It is measured by what it makes possible for readers who have no other access to the work.

The practical consequence is a shift in what reviewers should ask. Not "is it faithful?", which is a question with no stable answer, but "what reading of the original does this translation embody, and is that reading worth having?" The second question is harder, because it requires the reviewer to have a reading of her own. That, perhaps, is why the first has lasted so long.
